The empirical scope is too limited for the broad generalization claims. Important baselines and controls are missing, including oracle-mask training, oracle reference selection, random or alternative quality-based selection, and direct input masking versus 3D Gaussian pruning. Adapting scene-specific methods merely by inserting their masks into MVSplat may not constitute a fully competitive implementation of those approaches.

The central method is insufficiently specified. The paper never gives a complete definition of the final refined mask M; the entity-filling threshold and operation, precise robust-mask settings, scoring of differently generated reference/query masks, and the rule for detecting common occlusions during pruning are omitted.

The key premise that low self-rendering residual identifies static reference regions is not adequately validated. Because the references themselves generate the Gaussians, distractors may also be reconstructed with low residual; no analysis establishes mask precision under this failure mode.

Reproducibility is poor: several essential dataset, training, baseline, and implementation details are deferred to an appendix that is absent from the submitted PDF, while code and models are only promised. Runtime numbers also omit hardware, resolution, and a clear accounting of segmentation preprocessing.

Overall, the task formulation and numerical results are promising, but the contribution is largely a composition of heuristic masking, selection, and pruning operations, and the missing methodological details and evaluation controls prevent the central claims from being considered convincingly established.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: feed-forward, cross-scene 3D Gaussian reconstruction in the presence of transient distractors.
The reference-consistency masking idea is intuitive, technically plausible, and combined into a coherent framework covering training-time robustness, reference selection, and Gaussian pruning.

Results are consistently favorable. On the five-scene RobustNeRF average, DGGS obtains 21.74 PSNR versus 19.29 for the strongest adapted distractor baseline and 20.03 for pretrained MVSplat; held-out On-the-go and synthetic experiments show similar improvements.

weaknesses: The central claim that its masks outperform scene-specific methods is supported only qualitatively. Ground-truth mask metrics such as IoU, precision, and recall are absent, and reconstruction metrics do not establish mask accuracy.

The inference comparison is not fully controlled: DGGS selects four references from a pool of eight deliberately containing some relatively clean views, whereas most baselines receive only four references. Testing eight-reference DGGS-TR is not a substitute for random, segmentation-based, residual-based, or oracle top-four selection baselines. Constructing each pool around the evaluation query also makes practical generalization unclear.
Several named baselines are partial adaptations rather than faithful implementations; for example, the NeRF-HuGS adaptation removes Nerfacto. This weakens claims of superiority over those methods.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the statement: code is only promised, and important details are missing, including the exact final-mask construction, entity-filling thresholds, visibility handling during warping, common-occlusion pruning rule, loss weighting, optimizer and sampling configuration, and synthetic-dataset sizes and seeds. Equation 7 also has malformed summation notation.

The claimed plug-and-play generality is demonstrated only with MVSplat. Applying DGGS to another generalizable backbone, reporting multiple training seeds or uncertainty, and using a less engineered reference-pool protocol would materially strengthen the evidence.

The method is primarily a careful combination of established residual masking, pretrained segmentation, geometric warping, reference ranking, and primitive pruning; thus its methodological novelty is moderate, and the simplistic pasted-COCO synthetic data offers limited evidence for realistic occlusions and dynamics.

The central idea of using relatively reliable reference-view re-rendering and multiview consistency to correct residual-based masks is intuitive and technically plausible. Reference scoring and Gaussian pruning address complementary inference-time failure modes.

The reported improvements are substantial: the five-scene mean PSNR rises from 15.45 for retrained MVSplat to 21.02 for DGGS-TR and 21.74 for the complete method, with generally consistent SSIM and LPIPS improvements.

The component ablations cover mask prediction, refinement, auxiliary loss, reference scoring, pruning, segmentation alternatives, mask fusion, and input-set size. The paper also reports efficiency, synthetic transfer, qualitative results, and representative failure cases.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too small and insufficiently transparent for the broad generalization claims. Only two scenes are individually reported in the main five-scene comparison, the stated RobustNeRF scene count is inconsistent, and full DGGS results are omitted on the held-out On-the-go scenes because their evaluation views contain distractors. No multi-seed variation or uncertainty is reported.

The inference evaluation appears favorable to reference selection: candidate pools are formed around each query and deliberately include both distractor-containing and relatively clean images. Performance is not characterized as the clean-frame proportion, distractor coverage, or candidate-selection policy varies, nor is there a strong random/nearest/oracle selection comparison under the same candidate budget.

A central claim—that feed-forward masks outperform scene-specific methods—is supported only qualitatively. The synthetic setup provides exact distractor masks, yet the paper reports no mask IoU, precision, recall, or boundary accuracy. Thus the claimed mask superiority and attribution of reconstruction gains to more accurate masking remain inadequately established.

Several comparisons are not faithful implementations of the cited methods: scene-specific systems are reduced to transplanted masking components inside MVSplat, and NeRF-HuGS explicitly omits Nerfacto. These are useful engineering baselines but do not justify broad superiority claims over the original methods.

The synthetic benchmark uses independently positioned and rotated 2D COCO cutouts rather than physically consistent 3D distractors, and its number of scenes, splits, and construction details are unspecified. Consequently, its very large gains provide limited evidence about realistic dynamic occlusion.

Reproducibility and technical precision are below the top-tier threshold: code is only promised after publication; key thresholds, preprocessing, loss weighting, pruning rules, fine-tuning schedules, and timing accounting are missing or ambiguous. Equations for mask fusion/scoring and the pruning procedure are under-specified, while notation and dataset-count inconsistencies further impede replication. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but the unsupported mask claim, curated/narrow evaluation, and incomplete specification place the work marginally below acceptance.
